I am seventy years old, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou since I was strong enough to hold a hoe. I never went to school — I cannot read the words on a fertilizer bag — but I know this land, its seasons, and its demands better than any book. My family has eight *mu* of flat, good soil on the North China Plain, and like my father and his father before him, I grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation. That is the only system that makes sense here; the frost comes in winter and the heat comes in summer, and the wheat-maize double crop uses every day God gives us.

The wheat went into the ground last October, before the heavy cold. I rotary-tilled the land myself, turning the stubble from last year’s maize back into the soil, and sowed improved wheat seed — the kind they sell at the township seed station, a reliable variety that stands up to the wind and the dry spells. Now it is early spring, the wheat is waking up from its winter sleep, and I must act quickly. I will topdress it with urea when the greening starts, and then irrigate it three more times before June — once at jointing, once at heading, and once when the grain is filling. I also gave it a winter irrigation before the deep freeze, so that makes four times total. I will spray herbicide once to keep the weeds down, insecticide once when the aphids come, and fungicide once if the spring is damp. I expect about 470 *jin* per *mu* — a decent harvest if the weather holds.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant summer maize the same day or the next. Time is short; the frost will return by October. I use Denghai 605 hybrid seed — it costs more, but the yield is strong and the kernels fill well. I will not till for the maize; I sow directly into the wheat stubble with a no-till planter. The soil keeps its moisture, and at my age I cannot afford to waste labor on tillage in the burning summer heat. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea at the big-flare stage. I irrigate twice — once after sowing if the sky stays dry, and once at tasseling when the pollen needs cool moisture. I spray herbicide once, insecticide twice for the corn borer, and watch for disease. If all goes well, I will get about 580 *jin* per *mu* of maize.

I do not experiment. I do what has always worked, what my neighbors do, and what my bones tell me the weather will allow. This year will be no different.
